newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says EMU a matter of survival for Italy.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says EMU a matter of survival for Italy.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Friday said Italy had to meet the conditions for membership of the European Union's planned single currency "at all costs" and would not flinch from more budget cuts this year if necessary.

In a speech to a political party congress, the centre-left leader also said a free-spending past had left Italy with a mountain of debt that it could no longer afford and he signalled that the country's generous welfare system had to be slimmed.

"To those who ask me what is at stake in these years I have no hesitation in saying the destiny of the country and its very survival among the great nations of the world," Prodi told the meeting of the Popular Party, a partner in his coalition.
"To those who ask me why we have to enter Europe, I reply: because that is an essential condition for winning our wager, the wager with the future."
Since taking office in May, Prodi has pushed two budget packages through parliament to try to contain the public deficit.
A mid-year budget in 1996 was followed by a tough 62.5 trillion lire ($40.5 billion) package of measures for 1997 that includes an unpopular one-off "Euro-tax" levy on incomes.
The "Euro-tax" and other revenue-raising elements in the 1997 budget are designed to try to help Italy lower its annual deficit to the maximum 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.
The target is essential for countries wanting to join the EU's economic and monetary union (EMU) from its start in January, 1999. "It must be reached at all costs," Prodi said.
The odds on more budget cuts in the coming months shortened last week with figures showing a 1996 deficit of 138.5 trillion lire, 15.5 trillion more than the government had forecast.
"If a new adjustment budget should prove necessary next spring, and I still hope it will not be necessary, the government will not hesitate to draft it," Prodi said.

"I have also said, however, that if a budget is needed it will be on the spending side. Our attention in future action on economic policy must be primarily focused on structural reforms to spending and to its most severe control," he said.
Economists say Prodi must act soon on a mini-budget to maximise its impact, rather than wait as he has suggested for official quarterly accounts to be finalised in March.

European Commissioner Mario Monti, an Italian, joined the chorus of calls for faster action on Friday, telling Corriere della Sera newspaper in an interview that the sooner the measures were in place the better.
Monti said Italy should also speed up a review of its generous pension system. "It's hard to see why we don't bring things forward to 1997 since it's a key year," he said.

A review of a landmark 1995 pension reform deal is not due until 1998 but Prodi wants to begin early. Trades unions and Communist Refoundation, the hard-left party that is a key government ally, are vehemently opposed.
Prodi said the welfare state had to be realigned to changed conditions after decades of Italians "living beyond our means" by deficit spending.
"Each year this mountain of debts costs us 195 trillion lire in interest, a figure we can no longer sustain," he said.
Officials of some of Italy's EU partners say privately that past profligacy does not augur well for the country's chances of joining EMU as a founder member.
"Being inside or outside Europe must be the result of our actions. We want to be judged on them," Prodi said.
"The judgment on Italy cannot depend on what suits domestic policy in other European countries, however big they are."

Prodi did not elaborate but the remarks again signalled Italian sensitivity that some EU partners, including Germany, would prefer Italy not to be among EMU founder members because lira involvement would weaken the new euro currency. ($1=1539 Lire)
